title: Two traveling together
hookLine: the Shikoku pilgrimage around Kukai's island, walked by pilgrims in white
carry: two traveling together: kukai walks with the pilgrim

lines: AN ORANGE ON A COUNTRY ROAD.
A ROAD THAT COMES BACK AROUND.
cards: On a country road in Japan, an old woman steps out of her house and holds out an orange to a stranger.

The stranger is dressed all in white, with a wide sedge hat, a wooden staff, and a little bell that rings with each step. The stranger bows, takes the orange, and walks on. The woman goes back inside.

Neither of them thinks this is odd. On this island, people in white have been walking past front doors like hers for a very long time, on a road that goes all the way around and comes back to where it started.

teach.b: First, the teacher behind the road. Kukai, also known as Kobo Daishi, is the teacher tradition credits with bringing the esoteric teaching called Shingon to Japan, and Shikoku is the island tradition calls his home.
The pilgrimage follows temples linked with him, in a great loop around the island. The pilgrim is called a henro. Second, the clothes.
The white jacket is the mark of a pilgrim.

teach.h: WHITE CLOTHES, A STAFF, A HAT.
teach.b: Some say white was chosen because it's the color of burial clothes, so a pilgrim sets out ready for anything the road brings. The staff, tradition says, stands for Kukai himself. Third, two on the road.
Some pilgrims' hats carry words that mean two traveling together: the pilgrim may walk alone, but the teaching says Kukai walks beside them the whole way.
So at night, tradition says, pilgrims wash the tip of the staff before their own feet, caring for their companion first.
And at each temple, a pilgrim chants, leaves a slip with their name, and has a book stamped with a red seal and brushed with ink.
Fourth, the people along the way. Islanders offer pilgrims small gifts, an orange, tea, a ride, a bed. It's called osettai, and the pilgrim receives it as given to Kukai, not to themselves.
Some walk the whole loop at once. Others come back a section at a time, over years. Some go by bus or car.
However they go, the road brings them back to the temple where they began.

how: Pilgrims on Shikoku, often dressed in white with a hat and staff, visit the temples of the circuit on foot, by bus or by car, chanting at each one and collecting a red seal in a pilgrim's book, while islanders offer them small gifts called osettai.

o: a set of temples built in one city by a king
a vow to visit a new temple every week of the year
the pilgrim loop around Shikoku, Kukai's island

games.q: the Shikoku pilgrimage: tap the pairs.

s: pilgrims must walk the whole loop at once

games.q: you're a pilgrim at the end of a long day's walk. you have one basin of water. what do you wash first?
games.why: tradition says pilgrims wash the staff first, because it stands for Kukai, the companion who walks the road with them.

practice: If your space allows, choose a little circle, around a room, a table or a yard, and walk it slowly with an easy breath, letting whoever you hold dear walk beside you, like the two traveling together.
When you come back to where you started, stop and bow, or simply stand still. If walking isn't possible, trace a slow circle with your hand.

wordCard.voice: Eighty-eight temples. The pilgrimage around Shikoku, Kukai's island, walked by pilgrims in white who, tradition says, never walk alone. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: two traveling together: Kukai walks with the pilgrim. And the circle comes back home. See you tomorrow.
